screens.title: Variables, Data Types, and Operators
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn the building blocks of every Java program: variables, data types, and operators. A variable is a named storage location that holds a value; a data type tells Java what kind of value is stored and how much memory it needs. You will see the common primitive types — integers, floating-point numbers, characters, and booleans — and learn when to choose each type. We will also practice type casting, distinguishing automatic widening from explicit narrowing that can truncate data. Operators are the tools you use to compute, compare, and combine values: arithmetic for math, relational for comparisons, logical for boolean logic, assignment for updating values, and increment/decrement for small changes. Throughout the chapter you will encounter common pitfalls, like integer division that discards decimals, and the difference between prefix and postfix increments. Finally, you will apply these ideas in a simple BMI calculation to see types and operators working together. By the end you should be able to declare and initialize variables clearly, pick appropriate primitive types, perform safe casts, and reason about expression evaluation.

screens.title: What is a Variable?
screens.narratorSegment: A variable is a named memory location that holds a value which can change during program execution. When you declare a variable in Java you tell the compiler the variable's data type and name; this reserves appropriate memory and sets the rules for what operations are allowed. For example, declaring int count; reserves space for a 32-bit integer, while int count = 5; both declares and initializes it. Naming conventions matter: use lowercase and camelCase for multi-word names, like totalAmount, because readable names prevent misunderstandings later. A common misconception is to think declaration implicitly sets a useful default value; for local variables Java does not provide a default — you must initialize before use. Another confusion is using the wrong type: declaring a variable as int when you need decimals will silently discard fractional data if you later perform integer arithmetic. Concrete example: if you need to track people in a room use int; for a price use double. Practice habit: declare with an initialization when practical and pick a name that describes the role, not the storage. What small change could make your next variable name clearer?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A variable names memory and its declared type sets storage size and permitted operations.

content.html:
Core Concept

Variable declaration & initialization

Declaring reserves memory with a type and name; initializing assigns the first value. Good names reduce mistakes.

Example
int age = 30;
double price = 19.99;
char initial = 'A';
boolean isOpen = true;
Key Takeaway

Always pick a type that matches the value and initialize local variables before use to avoid compilation errors.

Why it matters
  • Type determines what operations are legal and how much memory is used.
  • Good naming helps collaborators and avoids accidental reuse of variables.
  • Initialization prevents runtime surprises and compiler errors for local variables.
Common mistake
Assuming a local variable has a default value; Java requires explicit initialization for locals.
Pro tip
Initialize where you declare when a sensible value exists; it improves readability and safety.
Quick scenario
If you store a quantity of items, int is appropriate. If you track currency, prefer double for accuracy among primitives. Ask: will fractional values occur?

screens.title: Primitive Data Types Overview
screens.narratorSegment: Java's primitive data types are the foundation for storing simple values. Integer types include byte, short, int, and long, each with progressively larger ranges and memory sizes. Use byte or short only when memory constraints really matter, int for most whole-number counts, and long when numbers can exceed two billion. Floating-point types are float and double; double is the preferred default for decimals because of better precision. Use float only when you need to reduce memory and can tolerate lower precision. The char type holds a single 16-bit Unicode character and is written in single quotes. Boolean stores true or false and is essential for control flow. A common misconception is to use float to save small amounts of memory for everyday computations; double is usually the safer choice. Concrete examples: int count = 42; double price = 19.99; char grade = 'A'; boolean isOpen = true. Notice that choosing the right primitive affects both correctness and performance in large arrays or computations. Which primitive will you choose for a counter that might exceed two billion? Primitive Data Types Overview means integers for whole numbers, floating-point for decimals, char for single characters, and boolean for truth values; pick based on range and precision.. In practical terms, integer types, floating-point, char, and boolean — when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition

Integer Types

byte (8-bit), short (16-bit), int (32-bit), long (64-bit). Use int for most counters; use long for very large totals.
Examples
byte b = 100;
short s = 30000;
int count = 2_000_000_000;
long bigNumber = 10000000000L;
Definition

Floating & Others

float (32-bit) and double (64-bit). char is a 16-bit Unicode character. boolean represents true or false.
Examples
float f = 19.99f;
double price = 19.99;
char initial = 'A';
boolean isOpen = false;
Comparison & guidance
  • Use int for everyday whole numbers; it balances size and range.
  • Use double for decimal calculations among primitive types; it minimizes precision surprises.
  • Use long when values could exceed int range, such as timestamps or large counters.
  • Use char for single characters and boolean for true/false decisions.
Common mistake
Choosing float to save memory for everyday calculations instead of double and encountering precision issues.
Scenario
For measuring money, use double among primitives, but be aware of rounding; in production, a decimal type like BigDecimal is preferred.
Key Takeaway
Match type to range and precision needs. Default to int and double unless you have a strong reason otherwise.

screens.title: Type Casting: Widening and Narrowing
screens.narratorSegment: Type casting converts a value from one primitive type to another. Widening conversions occur automatically when a smaller type is assigned to a larger compatible type: for example, assigning an int to a double gives you a double representation with no data loss. Narrowing conversions require an explicit cast because the target type may not hold the entire value; for example, casting a double to an int truncates the decimal portion. A concrete example: double myDouble = 9.78; int myInt = (int) myDouble; results in myInt being 9. Another dangerous example is overflow: int largeInt = 200; byte myByte = (byte) largeInt; yields an overflowed negative byte value. The misconception is thinking casts round values; narrowing casts truncate, and numeric overflow wraps according to the target range. When casting, always ask: can any meaningful information be lost? If yes, check and adjust your code. Try casting in small experiments and print the before and after values to build an intuition for truncation and overflow. Type Casting: Widening and Narrowing means widening is implicit and safe; narrowing is explicit and can truncate or overflow, so inspect values before casting.. In practical terms, how values convert automatically or explicitly and when data loss happens. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Casting rules
keyIdea.text: Widening is implicit and safe; narrowing is explicit and can truncate or overflow, so inspect values before casting.

content.html:
Process Flow

Widening (implicit)

Smaller to larger compatible type happens automatically. No cast operator needed.
int myInt = 10;
double myDouble = myInt; // becomes 10.0

Narrowing (explicit)

Larger to smaller requires a cast and may truncate or overflow.
double d = 9.78;
int i = (int) d; // i == 9 (decimal truncated)

int largeInt = 200;
byte b = (byte) largeInt; // overflow: b == -56
Key points
  • Widening preserves value; narrowing can truncate decimals or wrap due to range overflow.
  • Casting does not round; it truncates toward zero for floating to integer conversions.
  • Always validate values before narrowing casts when correctness matters.
Common mistake
Assuming a cast will round to the nearest integer. It truncates, losing the fractional part.
Check your understanding
Predict the values before running short examples: what does (int) -3.99 produce? What happens when you cast 260 to a byte?
Key Takeaway

Use widening freely; require explicit narrowing and check for truncation or overflow.

screens.title: Arithmetic Operators and Integer Division
screens.narratorSegment: Arithmetic operators let you compute numbers: plus, minus, times, divide, and modulus for remainders. A crucial concept is that the types of the operands determine the kind of division performed. If both operands are integers, Java performs integer division and discards any fractional part. For example, 5 / 2 using two ints yields 2, not 2.5. To get a decimal result you must have a floating-point operand, such as 5.0 / 2 or cast one operand to double. The modulus operator returns the remainder after division and is useful for parity checks or extracting digits. Concrete example: int result = 5 / 2; // result == 2; double precise = (double)5 / 2; // precise == 2.5. A common misconception is to trust implicit conversion after the division; if you assign an integer division result to a double, the fractional part is already lost. Always ensure at least one operand is floating-point before dividing when you expect decimals. Try converting one operand or both to practice predictable outcomes. Arithmetic Operators and Integer Division means operand types determine division behavior; integer division truncates decimals—use casting or floating operands for precise results.. In practical terms, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, modulus — and the integer division trap. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Operand types determine division behavior; integer division truncates decimals—use casting or floating operands for precise results.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Division examples

int a = 5;
int b = 2;
int result = a / b; // result == 2

double precise = (double) a / b; // precise == 2.5

double also = a / 2.0; // also == 2.5
Note that assigning result to a double after integer division does not recover the lost fraction.
Modulus and use cases
The modulus operator returns the remainder. It's useful for checking even/odd, wrapping indices, and extracting digits.
int r = 5 % 2; // r == 1
boolean isEven = (number % 2) == 0;
Common mistake
Expecting decimal results from two integer operands. Ensure one operand is floating-point when decimals are required.
Key Takeaway

Be explicit about operand types for division: cast or use a floating operand to preserve fractional parts.

screens.title: Relational Operators and Equality
screens.narratorSegment: Relational operators compare values and produce a boolean result: equal, not equal, greater than, or less than. For primitives like int or double, operators such as == and!= compare values directly. For example, 5 == 5 is true. A critical safety note is that when you later compare objects, the equality operator compares memory addresses, not content; that subtlety will come in later chapters. For now, focus on primitives: use relational operators to build conditions for control flow and loops. Concrete example: if (score >= passingScore) { pass = true; } Another common error is relying on equality for floating-point values because precision differences can make == behave unexpectedly; prefer threshold comparisons for floats and doubles in numeric algorithms. Practice by writing simple comparisons and predicting boolean outcomes, then test them in short programs to confirm your expectations. Which comparison will you need if you want to include equality when testing a range? Relational Operators and Equality means use relational operators for primitives; be cautious with floating-point equality and remember object equality differs from primitive equality.. In practical terms, comparing primitives and the future caution for objects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Relational rules
keyIdea.text: Use relational operators for primitives; be cautious with floating-point equality and remember object equality differs from primitive equality.

content.html:
Comparison

Relational operators

int x = 10;
int y = 7;
boolean eq = (x == y); // false
boolean ge = (x >= y); // true
Use these to drive if statements and loops, and test your conditions with simple inputs.
Floating equality caution
Floating-point arithmetic can produce small differences; avoid exact equality checks. Use a tolerance when comparing decimals.
double a = 0.1 + 0.2;
double b = 0.3;
// a == b might be false due to precision
boolean close = Math.abs(a - b) < 1e-9;
Note: object equality will be covered later. For primitives, relational operators compare contents directly.

screens.title: Logical Operators and Short-Circuiting
screens.narratorSegment: Logical operators let you combine boolean expressions into more complex conditions. The logical AND operator returns true only when both operands are true; the logical OR returns true when at least one operand is true; NOT inverts a boolean. Java also uses short-circuit evaluation: for &&, if the left operand is false, the right operand is not evaluated; for ||, if the left operand is true, the right is skipped. This behavior is useful to prevent errors and improve performance. For example, when checking an object for null before accessing a field, place the null check first so the second expression is not evaluated if the object is null. A concrete example: if (obj!= null && obj. isReady()) {... } will avoid a null pointer situation because the right side is only evaluated when the left is true. A common misconception is that both sides always evaluate; short-circuiting means they may not. Practice by writing expressions that rely on short-circuit to be safe, and ask: does evaluation order protect you from exceptions? Logical Operators and Short-Circuiting means use && and || to combine checks safely; structure expressions so short-circuiting prevents invalid evaluations.. In practical terms, combine boolean expressions safely using &&, ||, and !. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Short-circuiting examples

AND (&&)

}
Left false prevents right evaluation, avoiding exceptions and saving work.
OR (||)

screens.title: Assignment Operators & Compound Assignment
screens.narratorSegment: Assignment operators store values into variables. The simple assignment operator sets a variable equal to an expression. Compound assignment operators combine an operation with assignment, like +=, -=, *=, /=, and %=, and they update the variable in place. For example, x += 5 is equivalent to x = x + 5. These shorthands are convenient and often clearer. Be mindful of type rules: when using compound assignment with mixed types, Java applies implicit casting rules; for instance, an int plus a short may be promoted during computation. Increment and decrement operators, ++ and --, change a variable by one and come in prefix and postfix forms. The prefix form increments before the value is used, while the postfix uses the original value and then increments. Example: int a = 5; int b = a++; // b == 5, a == 6; int c = ++a; // a == 7, c == 7. A common mistake is confusing prefix and postfix in complex expressions; keep expressions simple or split steps for clarity. Compound assignment

screens.title: Operator Precedence and Associativity
screens.narratorSegment: Operator precedence and associativity determine how Java evaluates expressions with multiple operators. Precedence is the order operators are grouped; for example, multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction. Associativity decides how operators of the same precedence are grouped: most binary operators associate left-to-right. Parentheses override both rules and are the easiest way to make intent explicit. A practical example: 5 + 2 * 3 evaluates to 11 because multiplication has higher precedence, while (5 + 2) * 3 evaluates to 21 because parentheses change grouping. Another subtle point is that assignment is right-associative, so a = b = 5 sets both variables to 5. Misreading associativity leads to bugs in chained operations. Whenever you write a multi-operator expression, ask whether the default grouping matches your intent; if not, add parentheses. Practice by predicting outcomes and then running small programs to confirm evaluation order. BMICalculator template

public class BMICalculator {

    // 1. Declare and initialize variables for weight (kg) and height (m)

    double heightM = 1.75;  // example

    // 2. Calculate BMI using the formula: BMI = weight (kg) / (height (m) * height (m))
    double bmi = weightKg / (heightM * heightM);

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will learn the building blocks of every Java program: variables, data types, and operators. A variable is a named storage location that holds a value; a data type tells Java what kind of value is stored and how much memory it needs. You will see the common primitive types — integers, floating-point numbers, characters, and booleans — and learn when to choose each type. We will also practice type casting, distinguishing automatic widening from explicit narrowing that can truncate data. Operators are the tools you use to compute, compare, and combine values: arithmetic for math, relational for comparisons, logical for boolean logic, assignment for updating values, and increment/decrement for small changes. Throughout the chapter you will encounter common pitfalls, like integer division that discards decimals, and the difference between prefix and postfix increments. Finally, you will apply these ideas in a simple BMI calculation to see types and operators working together. By the end you should be able to declare and initialize variables clearly, pick appropriate primitive types, perform safe casts, and reason about expression evaluation.

In this set of objectives you will see the core skills to practice and why they matter. First, you will declare and initialize variables using clear names and appropriate types; this prevents bugs and communicates intent. Second, you will distinguish Java's primitive types, learning when to use byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, and boolean so your programs are both correct and efficient. Third, you will practice type casting: understand automatic widening that preserves value and explicit narrowing that can truncate or overflow, and learn how to predict those effects. Fourth, you will apply arithmetic, relational, and logical operators to build expressions and conditional checks. Each objective includes a short example and a competency milestone so you know when you have demonstrated the skill. Treat these objectives as active promises: try short code snippets until the outcomes become predictable and repeatable.

These objectives focus on practice and safety. First, you will learn naming conventions and initialization best practices so your variables communicate intent and avoid accidental shadowing. Second, you will practice choosing appropriate types for real examples — for instance, prefer int for counts and double for precise decimals. Third, you will learn to reason about short-circuit evaluation in logical expressions to avoid unnecessary computation or null access. Fourth, you will practice operator precedence and associativity to predict complex expressions and use parentheses to make intent explicit. Each objective is paired with a small mnemonic or visual and a verified competency milestone to guide practice. Working through these will reduce bugs caused by integer division, unexpected truncation from narrowing casts, or misuse of prefix versus postfix increments. In practical terms, write code that avoids common beginner pitfalls. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A variable is a named memory location that holds a value which can change during program execution. When you declare a variable in Java you tell the compiler the variable's data type and name; this reserves appropriate memory and sets the rules for what operations are allowed. For example, declaring int count; reserves space for a 32-bit integer, while int count = 5; both declares and initializes it. Naming conventions matter: use lowercase and camelCase for multi-word names, like totalAmount, because readable names prevent misunderstandings later. A common misconception is to think declaration implicitly sets a useful default value; for local variables Java does not provide a default — you must initialize before use. Another confusion is using the wrong type: declaring a variable as int when you need decimals will silently discard fractional data if you later perform integer arithmetic. Concrete example: if you need to track people in a room use int; for a price use double. Practice habit: declare with an initialization when practical and pick a name that describes the role, not the storage. What small change could make your next variable name clearer?

Java's primitive data types are the foundation for storing simple values. Integer types include byte, short, int, and long, each with progressively larger ranges and memory sizes. Use byte or short only when memory constraints really matter, int for most whole-number counts, and long when numbers can exceed two billion. Floating-point types are float and double; double is the preferred default for decimals because of better precision. Use float only when you need to reduce memory and can tolerate lower precision. The char type holds a single 16-bit Unicode character and is written in single quotes. Boolean stores true or false and is essential for control flow. A common misconception is to use float to save small amounts of memory for everyday computations; double is usually the safer choice. Concrete examples: int count = 42; double price = 19.99; char grade = 'A'; boolean isOpen = true. Notice that choosing the right primitive affects both correctness and performance in large arrays or computations. Which primitive will you choose for a counter that might exceed two billion? In practical terms, integer types, floating-point, char, and boolean — when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Type casting converts a value from one primitive type to another. Widening conversions occur automatically when a smaller type is assigned to a larger compatible type: for example, assigning an int to a double gives you a double representation with no data loss. Narrowing conversions require an explicit cast because the target type may not hold the entire value; for example, casting a double to an int truncates the decimal portion. A concrete example: double myDouble = 9.78; int myInt = (int) myDouble; results in myInt being 9. Another dangerous example is overflow: int largeInt = 200; byte myByte = (byte) largeInt; yields an overflowed negative byte value. The misconception is thinking casts round values; narrowing casts truncate, and numeric overflow wraps according to the target range. When casting, always ask: can any meaningful information be lost? Arithmetic operators let you compute numbers: plus, minus, times, divide, and modulus for remainders. A crucial concept is that the types of the operands determine the kind of division performed. If both operands are integers, Java performs integer division and discards any fractional part. For example, 5 / 2 using two ints yields 2, not 2.5.
